title: To Love a Place, and Speak for It
html:
Love for a place acquires a different weight when its people are waiting. Someone is waiting for work, someone for a home, someone for an office to answer a request that has already consumed too much of a life. Odisha at the Crossroads begins in the space between what a state hopes to become and what a person needs today. Pradeep Biswal brings to that space the experience of public service and the attentiveness of a poet.

An older voice in Odia poetry gives service a bodily, unforgettable image. In Bandira Atmakatha, Gopabandhu Das writes:

ମିଶୁ ମୋର ଦେହ ଏ ଦେଶମାଟିରେ,
ଦେଶବାସୀ ଚାଲିଯାଆନ୍ତୁ ପିଠିରେ ।
Let my body mingle with this country’s soil;
let my countrymen walk upon my back.
— Gopabandhu Das

Written within the struggle for swaraj, these lines imagine belonging through what one is willing to give. They offer an ethical horizon for reading a contemporary book about the common good. The circumstances have changed; the question of responsibility endures. What does affection for one’s country ask of a person who can see where others are being failed?

Biswal approaches that question through particular concerns: public money, institutions, livelihoods, housing, the use of land, the dignity of people growing old. His affection for Odisha stays close to the conditions in which its people live. A river belongs to memory and literature; it also belongs to the landscape on which lives depend. A town can be loved for its familiar streets while its planning and its treatment of residents demand scrutiny.

His poetry makes room for this questioning voice. The closing appeal in Where are You Now? is direct:

Come Bharat
Come sometime
We have many more
To discuss.
— Pradeep Biswal

The country is called into a conversation. The invitation is intimate, but it carries unfinished business. That combination helps us recognise the writer of these essays: someone who wishes to remain in dialogue with the place he loves, including when the conversation becomes uncomfortable. Concern can speak plainly. Loyalty can ask for an account of what has happened to a promise.

There is room in such a life for pleasure: the company of friends, the discovery of a poem, the daily renewal of a familiar landscape. These pleasures give public questions their human importance. Work should leave room for a person to live; a home should offer security; old age should retain companionship and self-respect. To celebrate life fully is to notice whose opportunities for celebration are narrowed by exclusion, anxiety or neglect.

His care for language belongs to this same attention. Odia carries the voices, memories and literary arguments through which a place knows itself. His writing in Odia and English makes that attachment available to different circles of readers. The two languages can carry a shared concern without becoming interchangeable. The question running beneath his literary and public work is how an inheritance can remain alive while its people claim a better future.

The essays begin with the state we imagine and move towards the institutions entrusted with it. From there they follow resources: how money is raised, shared and spent; how an announced intention may reach a household, an enterprise or a community. The sequence gives the reader time to pass from ambition to means and from means to consequences. Behind an allocation or a rule, a person’s life is taking shape.

The discussions of credit, skills, industry and transport bring opportunity into view. Those on cities, housing and regulation ask what happens when a reasonable hope meets an uncertain outcome. Mining, energy and the environment extend the circle of responsibility to the land and to those who will inherit it. Throughout, the reader is invited to examine benefits and burdens together, and to ask who has been heard before a decision is called progress.

Speaking up carries obligations of its own: to be clear, to attend to evidence, to distinguish a hope from an achievement and to allow a judgement to be reconsidered. These essays retain the dates and circumstances of their interventions wherever established. A later disappointment may stand beside an earlier expectation. Read together, they preserve the work of thought as it responds to events, with its urgency and its limits.

Towards the close, the discussion turns to unequal access, shared responsibility and care in later life. Here the scale of public purpose becomes as close as a household. Wordsworth, in Tintern Abbey, remembers:

His little, nameless, unremembered, acts
Of kindness and of love.
— William Wordsworth

Such acts give the common good a daily presence. They ask to be supported by institutions that are dependable, by services that reach people and by a public culture willing to listen. The movement from policy to an older person’s need for care brings the volume back to the individual life from which any meaningful account of development must begin.

The love of Odisha expressed here is both tender and demanding. It can take joy in what the state has given its people and remain restless about what its people are still denied. It asks us to live with gratitude, to question with care, and to lend our voices where silence would leave someone alone. A place is cherished through this continuing attention: in the language we keep alive, in the life we make possible for a neighbour, and in the future we are willing to answer for.

title: The State We Imagine
html: The opening essays consider the horizon of development: what Odisha hopes to become, which ideas about economic life it inherits, and what a neighbouring country’s experience might invite it to examine. These are starting points for enquiry. They prepare the questions that follow about institutions, resources and the responsibilities attached to public ambition.

title: Institutions Worthy of Trust
html: A public promise depends on the institutions that carry it. The discussion moves from principles of governance to planning, coordination, education and electoral trust. Each essay approaches a different part of that relationship. Together they ask how a citizen can recognise responsibility in the conduct of government and in the services it provides.

title: The Public Purse
html: Public work requires resources, and the way those resources are raised and shared affects what can be done. These essays move between state finances, Union transfers, local bodies and borrowing. Their subjects are connected, but their dates and jurisdictions differ. Keeping those distinctions in view allows the reader to follow the larger question of fiscal responsibility without losing the particular argument of each piece.

title: What We Choose to Fund
html: An allocation expresses a choice. This section follows the use of public money from a state budget to national taxation and budget priorities, then returns to Odisha’s spending decisions. The essays weigh immediate needs against longer ambitions. Their recurring concern is whether expenditure becomes something useful in people’s lives, and what other possibilities are set aside along the way.

editorialNote: The following essays move from Odisha’s 2025–26 budget to national tax legislation and the 2026 Union Budget, then to a proposal written before Odisha’s 2026–27 budget. Their sequence follows spending choices across levels of government.

title: Work, Skill and Opportunity
html: Opportunity needs more than a promise of growth. It may require a loan, a useful skill, a reliable connection to a market or conditions in which an enterprise can survive. The following essays move from banking and public enterprises towards transport, handloom, tourism and newer industries. Their sequence brings inherited strengths and future ambitions into the same conversation about work.

title: The Right to a Home
html: The promise of development becomes tangible in a neighbourhood and a home. Planning, affordability and the conduct of the property market shape that promise; regulation is tested when something goes wrong. This section moves from the growth of cities to the experience of homebuyers and the challenge of securing effective relief. Earlier and later assessments are kept in view together.

title: The Land We Must Leave
html: The land carries the consequences of development beyond the life of any single project. Mining, electricity and a changing climate connect present needs with responsibilities that extend into the future. These essays ask how Odisha can provide for its people while attending to the resources, communities and living environments on which that provision depends.

title: Development for Whom?
html: The last section returns to the people whose experience gives policy its purpose. Regional deprivation, women’s access to opportunity and the design of assistance lead towards a quieter concern: companionship and care in later life. The scale changes from a region to a household, while the question of dignity remains. Development must be felt by those in whose name it is pursued.
